prompt_version: s5-extract-facts-v2 (adapted from Paleo Atlas extract-facts-v3; v2 after Sofía's S5 review)

facts.statement: In cell lines and neurons, a tagged version of a 20-repeat arginine-rich peptide was quickly taken into the cells and moved to the nucleolus.
facts.subject: cells_or_tissue

facts.statement: Experiments using small molecules and RNA interference indicated that the peptide enters cells through a temperature-dependent fluid-phase endocytosis process.
facts.subject: cells_or_tissue

facts.statement: Researchers used iridium-labeled dipeptide repeat proteins to find candidate cell-surface proteins, which were then tested in a secondary RNA interference screen.
facts.subject: cells_or_tissue

facts.statement: Blocking the synthesis of glycosaminoglycan chains or reducing the levels of the protein CSPG4 lowered the amount of the peptide taken up by cells.
facts.subject: cells_or_tissue

facts.statement: Reducing the expression of CSPG4 protected neurons from the toxic effects caused by the 20-repeat peptide.
facts.subject: cells_or_tissue

facts.statement: A dual reporter system showed that a 50-repeat peptide made by one neuron easily spread to nearby neurons in a lab setting.
facts.subject: cells_or_tissue

facts.statement: Fluid from neurons expressing 50-repeat arginine or glycine peptides contained transmissible protein that entered other neurons in a way that depended on CSPG4.
facts.subject: cells_or_tissue

facts.statement: The findings suggest that CSPG4 plays a role in how these arginine-rich peptides are taken into cells and passed between them.
facts.subject: cells_or_tissue
